history.content: I was certain, until the story of Jensen Huang’s second affair hit, that Huang was bulletproof. After all, why wouldn’t he be? He’s placed himself indispensably at the center of the AI industry and famously had no succession plan at Nvidia. In fact, he’s the only CEO Nvidia has ever had. L’état c’est moi.Then two stories were published nearly back to back on Wednesday: one alleging Huang had an affair with his subordinate Kimberly Powell, another that the board was meeting to consider his ouster. First thing Thursday morning, Nvidia announced Huang had resigned. One of the most powerful men in Silicon Valley was out.Why throw Huang under the bus for getting his nuts drained?Fascinating. First of all, when I asked on Monday “Who else is Jensen Huang fucking?” I did not expect to get answers this fast — somebody, potentially somebody on the board (as we’ve seen in other incidents), wanted the story out there. Second, why throw Huang under the bus for getting his nuts drained? This is not an industry that cares about that kind of thing — just ask Eric Schmidt and Bill Gates. My guess is that the second affair is a pretext for action, and this all goes back to the original story from last week: that Huang was honeypotted by an alleged Chinese spy. Whatever was going on with neocloud Megaspeed might be much, much worse than we know, and what we know is pretty bad: business listings that led to “a Malaysian data center and shopping mall, a near-empty office in Singapore and a dilapidated storefront outside Kuala Lumpur.”Do you have information about Nvidia? Contact Elizabeth Lopatto securely on Signal at lopatto.46.Even months before the report that Alice “No Relation” Huang, an exec at Megaspeed, was having an affair with Huang, there were questions about Nvidia’s business in China. The US government has placed strict export controls on Nvidia’s high-end chips. Huang claimed in May that as a result, Nvidia has zero percent market share in China. But also in May, short sellers Culper Research published a report in which they wrote, “We believe that in reality, over 20% of Nvidia’s FY 2026 compute revenues remained driven by China – supported both by illegal GPU diversion and Southeast Asian intermediaries.”Megaspeed was Nvidia’s largest Southeast Asian buyer, but Singaporean newspaper The Straits Times visited Megaspeed’s Singapore office a month ago to find “no signs of activity.” Another building tenant told the reporters, “It is always dark for as long as it has been here. I hardly see anyone visiting or in the office.” The sole director of Megaspeed, Tan Yong Pong, appears to have vanished. The Singaporean company that owns Megaspeed, Swiftdata, has listed an office that belongs to an interior design firm as its business address.Megaspeed is only part of the storyIncidentally, Alice Huang has surfaced in Beijing. The Financial Times says she’s barred from Singapore for giving police “inaccurate information.” Oh, and reportedly her companies invested in Chinese AI company DeepSeek and promised them Nvidia’s Blackwell chips? Fun!Megaspeed is only part of the story, I think. There are two Chinese chip-related scandals that could cause serious problems for Nvidia, and both feature people with close ties to Huang. One is Megaspeed, which involves Huang’s maybe-spy affair partner. The other centers on Super Micro (which, horribly, does business as Supermicro), a partner of Nvidia run by one of Huang’s old friends, Charles Liang. Super Micro’s cofounder, Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw, along with Ruei-Tsang “Steven” Chang and Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun, allegedly defrauded the US by serving as a passthrough for a front company to buy $2.5 billion of Nvidia chips for Alibaba. The front company, not named in the indictment, is Thailand-based OBON, according to Bloomberg. Liang and Super Micro have not been charged.But these incidents may not be the end of Nvidia’s problems. Take for instance, more recently, New Matrix — another company that barely exists, and yet is an approved buyer of Nvidia chips. It is, in fact, one of several approved companies that “have ties to firms that have been blacklisted by the U.S. government, or that work as military contractors in China,” according to The New York Times.The question, of course, is how high this all goesHuang has insisted that Nvidia has seen “no evidence of any AI chip diversion.” He’s been pretty emphatic on that point, actually. I am now wondering if that is even a little bit true. If the board is cutting Huang loose, there’s probably more on chip smuggling allegations coming.More substantively, Nvidia reportedly intervened in a 2025 Commerce Department investigation of Megaspeed, which was suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips — halting the investigation. Since the scandal broke, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick appears to have become the fall guy for this, with Axios reporting that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent “confronted” him about failing to note Megaspeed as a national security concern and Politico saying “more than half a dozen Republicans have demanded answers” from him.The question, of course, is how high this all goes. After all, Huang was awfully buddy-buddy with President Donald Trump, who was informed about Huang’s maybe-spy girlfriend in 2025 and apparently did nothing about it. Incidentally, Nvidia has reportedly donated $25 million to Trump’s planned ballroom. This is what gangster tech regulation looks like.I wonder what else was an open secret at the company, you know?Come January, Elizabeth Warren will be able to send subpoenas in her role as the chair of the Senate Banking Committee. And wouldn’t you know, she seems to be pretty interested. Democrats will control both the House and the Senate. Their voters have given them a mandate to root out corruption. And boy howdy, does Nvidia look like a sitting duck right now. If Huang knew chips were being diverted — or had reason to know that — and tried to ensure their sales anyway, he may have committed actual crimes (bribery, espionage, smuggling, whatever) and, under a functioning legal system, could actually go to jail. Nvidia dispensing with its indispensable CEO is the company reducing its risk of getting roped into Huang’s drama.Will it be that easy for Nvidia? I wonder. The most interesting part of the second affair story, with Powell, the Nvidia vice president of healthcare, comes at the very end of the New York Times article. When someone took a video of Powell and Huang being “affectionate” in March, Huang’s security had nondisclosure agreements ready to go. CNBC reports that rumors of their affair have circulated “for years.” I wonder what else was an open secret at the company, you know? Especially since Huang had 60 direct reports, so every part of the company is covered in his fingerprints.Over in the tech world, people still seem to be in denial. On X, the social network for Trumpist dead-enders, the account “zerohedge” posted, “Elon please hire Jensen.” Elon Musk replied, “That would be an honor.”
history.author: Elizabeth Lopatto
history.descriptionZh:
这篇评论性报道围绕英伟达CEO黄仁勋的突然辞职展开。原文作者称，自己原本认为黄仁勋“不可替代”：他是英伟达唯一一任CEO，长期把自己置于AI产业中心，且公司没有公开的继任计划。但周三几乎同时出现两篇报道，一篇称黄仁勋与下属、英伟达医疗业务副总裁金伯利·鲍威尔存在婚外情，另一篇称董事会开会考虑罢免他；周四上午，英伟达宣布黄仁勋辞职。作者据此认为，婚外情可能只是采取行动的借口，真正背景要回到上周关于黄仁勋被指遭“中国间谍”以“美人计”接近的报道，以及英伟达芯片经东南亚中介流向中国的问题。原文带有强烈作者判断和推测，相关指控需以正式调查和司法结论为准。

文章称，Megaspeed是英伟达在东南亚最大的买家，也是新型云服务商（neocloud）。但新加坡《海峡时报》一个月前探访其新加坡办公室时发现“没有任何活动迹象”，同一楼内租户称该办公室“一直黑着，几乎看不到人来”。Megaspeed唯一董事Tan Yong Pong似乎已经消失；拥有Megaspeed的新加坡公司Swiftdata，其登记营业地址竟属于一家室内设计公司。商业登记信息还指向马来西亚一个数据中心和购物中心、新加坡近乎空置的办公室，以及吉隆坡郊外一处破败店面。与黄仁勋有婚外情传闻的Megaspeed高管Alice Huang已出现在北京；据《金融时报》，她因向警方提供“不准确信息”被新加坡禁止入境。报道还称，她的公司投资了中国AI公司DeepSeek，并承诺向其提供英伟达Blackwell芯片。

文章将Megaspeed视为英伟达中国业务风险的一部分。美国政府对英伟达高端芯片实施严格出口管制，黄仁勋5月称英伟达在中国市场份额已降至零。但同月，做空机构Culper Research发布报告称，“我们认为现实中，英伟达2026财年超过20%的计算收入仍由中国驱动——既包括非法GPU转运，也包括东南亚中介。”原文没有给出芯片性能参数或架构对比，核心争议是高端AI芯片如何通过第三方、空壳公司和东南亚节点流向中国。Blackwell在文中仅作为被承诺转运的高端芯片出现，原文未展开其技术原理或创新点。

文章称，Megaspeed只是问题的一部分。另一条线索涉及英伟达合作伙伴Super Micro：其联合创始人Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw、Ruei-Tsang “Steven” Chang和Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun被指通过一家前台公司作为中转，为阿里巴巴购买价值25亿美元的英伟达芯片，从而欺诈美国。据彭博社，这家未在起诉书中点名的主要公司是泰国公司OBON；梁见后（Charles Liang）和Super Micro本身未被起诉。还有New Matrix：这家公司几乎不存在，却是英伟达芯片的获批买家。据《纽约时报》，它只是多家获批公司之一，这些公司“与美国政府黑名单上的企业有关联，或在中国作为军工承包商开展业务”。

文章进一步称，英伟达曾干预美国商务部2025年对Megaspeed涉嫌走私英伟达芯片的调查，并叫停了调查。丑闻爆发后，商务部长霍华德·卢特尼克似乎成为替罪羊：Axios称财政部长斯科特·贝森特就未将Megaspeed列为国家安全关切“质问”卢特尼克；Politico称“超过六名共和党人要求他作出答复”。作者质疑问题会牵扯到多高层级，并提到黄仁勋与特朗普关系密切，特朗普在2025年已获知黄仁勋的“可能是间谍的女友”却似乎未采取行动；英伟达还据报道向特朗普计划中的舞厅捐赠2500万美元。作者称这是“黑帮式科技监管”。

在作者看来，黄仁勋一直坚称英伟达“没有发现任何AI芯片转运的证据”，但董事会与黄仁勋切割，可能是公司为降低被卷入其个人风波和法律风险的概率。文章称，明年1月伊丽莎白·沃伦将能以参议院银行委员会主席身份发出传票，而民主党将控制参众两院，其选民授权他们反腐，英伟达目前看起来风险很大。如果黄仁勋知道芯片被转运，或有理由知道却仍推动销售，他可能涉及贿赂、间谍、走私等实际犯罪，在正常法律体系下可能入狱。文章还提到，关于鲍威尔的第二篇婚外情报道在《纽约时报》文末称，3月有人拍到鲍威尔与黄仁勋“亲密”时，黄仁勋的安保团队已准备好保密协议；CNBC称两人的婚外情传闻已流传“多年”。黄仁勋有60名直接下属，作者因此怀疑公司内还有多少“公开的秘密”。科技界仍有否认情绪：X账号zerohedge发帖“Elon please hire Jensen”，马斯克回复“那将是荣幸”。

总体看，原文不是一篇芯片技术报道，未涉及GPU架构原理、性能参数或创新点对比；它主要讨论英伟达在出口管制、第三方转运、东南亚中介、公司治理和美国政治监督下的合规与法律风险。其技术影响在于：高端AI芯片出口管制执法和供应链透明度将成为AI算力产业的关键变量，东南亚数据中心、云服务商和空壳中介可能成为敏感节点；应用场景则涉及AI训练芯片、云算力服务和数据中心采购。原文提供的关键数据包括：黄仁勋称中国市场份额为零，Culper称2026财年超20%计算收入由中国驱动，Super Micro案涉25亿美元芯片，英伟达政治捐赠2500万美元，以及黄仁勋有60名直接下属。

history.content: Shoppers using AI chatbots to research products or find places to buy items could be directed to imposters and other risky websites, a new study found.The study conducted by IP protection firm Podqi and shared exclusively with The Verge prompted ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity with a handful of shopping-related questions involving a selection of 151 brands. Questions included “What are the top websites for buying [brand]?”; “Where can I find [brand] online?”; and “Does [brand] ship internationally? What are their regional websites?” The test ran over the course of two testing periods in September and asked about 151 small and large companies like fashion brands Lululemon, Birkenstock, Stüssy, and Madhappy (a client of Podqi) and homeware brand Le Creuset. Podqi crafted its own prompts (as opposed to using real user conversations) and tested its prompts using a tool that tracks AI answers across chatbots.Perplexity performed the worst, showing risky sites in 15 percent of answersOver the course of 6,795 answers, Podqi found that all three AI engines cited and showed shoppers risky sites, defined as fake websites impersonating real retailers or selling knockoffs, old brand domains that have been reregistered by someone else, or dead sites that aren’t active at all but that someone else could purchase and reuse. Google’s Gemini showed risky sites least often of the three, linking to or mentioning a risky site in 4 percent of answers. (Mentions include instances of recommending a risky site, displaying it without comment, and warning a user about it.) Perplexity performed the worst, showing risky sites in 15 percent of answers. ChatGPT fell somewhere in the middle at 8 percent. ChatGPT performed the best when it came to offering warnings about each risky site that it surfaced, doing so 24 percent of the time. Smaller brands appear especially at risk: Podqi found that queries related to larger companies had risky sites in answers about half as often.AI companies market chatbots as being helpful for shopping tasks like researching, comparing, and discovering products or retailers. AI citing fake sites is a headache for brands and retailers, of course, but it could also quickly become a risk for consumers. The issue could be especially relevant going into the upcoming holiday shopping season, when consumers are hunting around for in-stock items and the best prices. It’s likely that more consumers will be using AI to shop this year, including buying products from brands or sites they’re not already familiar with.“Part of this piece, too, is making sure that the consumers know, even though you are being fed a result in a particular chatbot, it is always best to verify the source of that before entering personal information or credit card information,” says Podqi CEO and cofounder Trevor West.“We take information quality seriously, and are happy to see that Gemini performed best among the products tested,” Google spokesperson Jessica Levis Boord said in an email. “We continually work to test and improve our models, and are upfront that Gemini is AI and can make mistakes, so we display links to sources alongside responses to help people verify information.”“Our goal is for ChatGPT to connect people with reliable places to shop,” OpenAI spokesperson Taya Christianson said in an email. “We’re continuing to improve our safeguards to make potentially deceptive sites less likely to appear in shopping-related results. We appreciate researchers sharing examples that show us where we can improve the experience.”In Podqi’s test, certain prompts seemed to trigger risky sites more often than others. For example, AI displayed risky sites more often when asked about regional brand websites compared to other prompt categories. The tested AI engines also at times listed fake regional sites for brands that do not have any. In one conversation, Perplexity named the wrong page as Stüssy’s official website and called it “the best starting point for guaranteed authentic items.”“Perplexity is consistently the most accurate AI on credible research benchmarks, and has been for four years. We never claim to be 100% accurate, but we do claim to be the only company relentlessly focused on it,” spokesperson Jesse Dwyer said in an email.

history.titleZh: 研究发现，AI聊天机器人正在推荐虚假零售网站
history.descriptionZh:
一项由知识产权保护公司Podqi开展、并与The Verge独家分享的研究发现，消费者使用AI聊天机器人研究商品或寻找购买渠道时，可能被引导至仿冒网站和其他高风险站点。研究在9月的两个测试期内，围绕151个品牌设计了购物相关问题，测试对象包括ChatGPT、Gemini和Perplexity。问题包括“购买某品牌的最佳网站有哪些”“在哪里可以在线找到某品牌”“某品牌是否支持国际配送、其地区网站是什么”等，覆盖Lululemon、Birkenstock、Stüssy、Madhappy和Le Creuset等大小品牌。Podqi使用自制提示词而非真实用户对话，并通过可跨聊天机器人追踪AI回答的工具进行测试。

研究共分析6795条回答，发现三家AI引擎都曾引用或展示高风险网站。所谓高风险网站包括：仿冒真实零售商的假网站、销售仿冒品的网站、被他人重新注册的旧品牌域名，以及已失效但可能被他人购买并重新启用的域名。结果显示，Google Gemini表现相对最好，在4%的回答中链接或提及高风险网站；ChatGPT为8%；Perplexity最差，达到15%。在对其展示的高风险网站发出警告方面，ChatGPT表现最好，警告比例为24%。研究还发现，小品牌面临的风险更高：涉及大公司的查询中，回答出现高风险网站的频率约为小品牌相关查询的一半。某些提示类型更容易触发高风险结果，尤其是询问品牌地区网站时；AI有时还会为根本没有地区网站的品牌列出虚假的地区站点。在一次对话中，Perplexity将错误页面列为Stüssy的官方网站，并称其是“确保正品的最佳起点”。

从技术上看，这一问题反映出生成式AI在购物场景中结合检索、引用和答案生成时，对网站实体匹配、来源可信度和授权销售渠道的验证仍不充分。模型可能把过期域名、仿冒站点或缺乏权威信号的小品牌页面当作可用来源；在地区站点、国际配送等意图下，查询歧义和索引质量问题会进一步放大风险。对品牌和零售商而言，AI引用假站不仅会造成流量和信任损失，也可能损害品牌形象；对消费者而言，风险在于误入假店、购买仿冒品，或在不可信网站输入个人信息和信用卡数据。随着假日购物季临近，消费者更可能使用AI寻找有货商品和低价商品，甚至购买不熟悉的品牌，因此该问题更具现实紧迫性。Podqi CEO兼联合创始人Trevor West建议，即使聊天机器人给出了结果，消费者在输入个人信息或信用卡信息前，仍应核实来源。

三家AI公司均作出回应。Google发言人Jessica Levis Boord表示，公司重视信息质量，对Gemini在测试产品中表现最好感到高兴，并称会持续测试和改进模型，同时明确Gemini是AI、可能出错，因此在回答旁显示来源链接以帮助用户核实。OpenAI发言人Taya Christianson表示，目标是让ChatGPT连接可靠的购物地点，并正在改进防护措施，使潜在欺骗性网站更少出现在购物相关结果中，同时感谢研究者提供改进案例。Perplexity发言人Jesse Dwyer则称，Perplexity四年来在可信研究基准上持续是最准确的AI，公司不声称100%准确，但声称是唯一持续专注准确性的公司。需要注意的是，该研究使用自制提示而非真实用户对话，且“提及”包括推荐、无评论展示和警告等不同情况，因此结果更适合作为风险暴露指标，而非AI购物回答总体错误率。总体而言，该研究提示AI购物助手在来源验证、地区站点识别和小品牌覆盖方面仍有明显短板，平台需加强防护和来源标注，品牌需监测AI答案并维护官方域名与渠道信息，消费者则应对AI推荐的购物网站进行交叉验证。

history.title: Jensen Huang is out. What did China want from him?
history.description:
Today, we’re talking about the Jensen Huang scandal at Nvidia, which is developing so quickly that we had to do an emergency update of this intro minutes before publishing this episode.

This happens all the time, and to anyone in Silicon Valley who’s trying to make this “neat” argument, all I can say is, go talk to people in China. They can tell you how messy it actually is on the ground.
Kyle, this has been great. What do you think will happen next year? What should people be looking out for?
The biggest thing is a congressional investigation and who’s behind that, what that surface is. And then potentially along with that, these pending bills around export controls and whether those will now get more momentum to pass in Congress, and whether Trump himself, and the White House in general, will try to play a role in either stopping that or giving that a quiet green light.
I suspect we’re going to want to talk to you again as this process plays out. Thank you so much, Kyle, for being on Decoder.
Thank you.

history.content: Today, we’re talking about the Jensen Huang scandal at Nvidia, which is developing so quickly that we had to do an emergency update of this intro minutes before publishing this episode.Huang just resigned from his position as CEO of Nvidia as news of his affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy, threatened to engulf the company.We’ll have more on that story as things develop and we learn how Nvidia will restructure itself after Jensen — he had something like 60 direct reports, after all, and the entire AI financial ecosystem flows through the company. This is pure Decoder bait.But just two days ago I talked to Kyle Chan, a foreign policy fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center, about the real heart of the scandal: What would China even seek to accomplish by having a spy so close to Jensen? And what does the real state of the US-China AI conflict really looks like, particularly from the Chinese point of view?Kyle’s answers about chips and how China is perceiving the so-called AI “race” were very illuminating, but maybe even more interesting was his observation on Jensen Huang’s relationship with Trump was the most important thing of all — because maybe what China most stood to gain was someone who could whisper in the right ears.Let’s just dive right into it. But keep in mind that when we were talking, we still didn’t know what would happen with Jensen.Okay: Kyle Chan on Nvidia, China, and the future of AI export controls. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.Kyle Chan, you are a fellow at the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution. Welcome to Decoder.Great to be here.What on earth could we be talking about as it relates to your expertise about China today? I have a lot to ask you about Nvidia, about our relationship to China as a country, as an economy, and about national security.Let’s start at the very beginning. From all the reporting we have today, it seems like the United States government has been very worried about a company called Megaspeed and Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy at the center of the swirling scandal around Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia. What do we know about Alice Huang and Megaspeed?We have to be careful about what we know and what we don’t know. So far, there are allegations that the US intelligence community believes that Alice Huang may be an asset of the Chinese intelligence services. Megaspeed itself is a customer of Nvidia’s and they built a data center in Malaysia.They also seem to potentially have ties with Chinese companies and could — and this is where we’re getting into what we do know and what we don’t know — potentially be a conduit for Chinese AI companies accessing cutting-edge Nvidia chips like Blackwells.Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.I want to rewind way back. The notion that the Chinese AI industry wants Nvidia chips has been floating around for years and the idea that the Chinese AI industry would somehow develop a parallel set of technology or a superior set of technology because of the constraint of not having Nvidia chips has percolated into the discourse several times.I’m particularly thinking about DeepSeek. DeepSeek launched R1 and it outperformed our models in some ways. We think they didn’t have access to the chips. There are some accusations that they had access to the chips. It turns out they did a bunch of fine-tuning on the chips they did have.What is that relationship like? Do they need the highest-end Nvidia chips? Is it true that they’re actually developing parallel technologies that might be superior to the chips they can have? Just set that stage.A lot of the details are murky, and they’re probably murky for a reason. But up until now, we saw Chinese AI companies that were very heavily dependent on Nvidia chips in order to train and run their models. In fact, they became some of the biggest contributors to the CUDA ecosystem, which is Nvidia’s software ecosystem and platform.They got very good at that, but at the same time with US export controls and greater technology restrictions on access to cutting-edge GPUs, China increasingly pushed these AI companies to switch away from Nvidia to Huawei and other domestic AI chip makers. The idea there is to develop a parallel domestic AI chip supply chain that is good enough, if not on par with, Nvidia’s latest chips, and — crucially — resilient to policy actions coming out of Washington.So that is the story up until this point. The question is, now, what is that trajectory for the Chinese GPU or AI chip development?The reason I wanted to start there is that the motivations to get close to Jensen Huang are very murky to me. As the CEO of Nvidia, I understand that everyone thinks he’s the character and he’s actually in the software designing the next generation of Nvidia GPUs, but he’s just traveling the world giving policy speeches.If you want to build a parallel GPU ecosystem, you’re trying to get close to the designers and the engineers, right? What would be the goal of trying to get close to Jensen Huang?If you wanted the design specs for the latest Nvidia GPUs, I don’t know if you would ask Jensen directly. I think you might want to go to his technical staff.He does have like 60 direct reports. Decoder is often a show about org charts and that one has been on top of my list for a long time, but we’ll set that aside for now. Keep going.What it’s really about is potentially two things. One is trying to understand, maybe to glean information about, the US policymaking process. Jensen Huang is very close to Trump. They talk a lot. Trump can apparently just call Jensen on his cell phone at any moment.In the middle of a conference. We’ve seen the video.On the other side, and maybe this is even the bigger issue, perhaps it’s the biggest concern of all, is the concern that the direction of movement could run the other way, which is that somehow through Jensen, China might be able to influence US policymaking, especially on export controls. That is the big worry from a lot of people in Washington.One of the other underlying concerns here, that I’m just trying to parse out, is that Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy, is an executive at a company called Megaspeed. And through Megaspeed, Nvidia may have already been circumventing export controls.It seems like if you’re already solving the problem, maybe you should just leave it alone. How does that dynamic play out?A lot of the story is strange. Even seen in the most cynical terms, it doesn’t quite add up. There could be several different possibilities. One is that this is actually not some concerted strategy from Beijing to try to obtain chips or information or influence, but this is potentially Beijing not quite understanding the full situation and wanting to co-op this Alice Huang person and at least try to understand from her standpoint what is happening.Because I think you’re right. Already you have a very strong relationship between Nvidia and Megaspeed. You also already have — and this is on the influence side — Jensen Huang advocating for his own commercial interests, for a loosening of export controls on his own chips to China. You don’t really need Beijing to push on that gas pedal. That’s already happening.So there are some things that don’t quite make sense if you’re thinking about it from those standpoints, but if you’re thinking about it from the viewpoint of “Beijing wants visibility,” then perhaps that is another plausible explanation.Beijing just wants someone who Trump calls on the phone to advocate for their viewpoints. I see all of that, but what are we getting out of it? If the goal is Nvidia chips, it feels like that is already assured. If the goal is Nvidia engineering plans, that feels like a question mark. If the goal is influence over the Trump administration, I feel like they could have just bought cryptocurrency.[Laughs] That’s right.There’s a big swirl of what is actually happening here. Maybe your point that Beijing just needed more visibility because it is a swirl is the motivating factor. The question that leads me to is that the New York Times reports that US intelligence agencies first flagged these issues a year ago to the Trump administration. There was a memo from Marco Rubio. The reporting is that he oversaw the memo, which is as much plausible deniability as anything. He oversaw it. He was aware that there was a memo. A year ago, the United States’ national security apparatus was worried about Alice Huang at Megaspeed, her relationship with Jensen, and nothing occurred. What do you make of that?That is one of the most worrying aspects of all this. Regardless of what the details are and what is known publicly versus what our intelligence community knows, this is something that should be investigated. This is obviously a major national security issue and this is something where you don’t want someone meddling with this process. You want to do a full investigation, get to the bottom of what’s happening.I think what we’re seeing from some of the reporting is that this has been known, and in fact, if anything, there may have been efforts to try to stop this investigation or distort it in some way. That is very troubling from that internal, within-the-US-government perspective.There’s a lot going on with Nvidia in that part of the story, where Nvidia’s own spokespeople are saying, “There’s nothing going on here. This is a normal relationship,” on the record to many publications. A week later, Jensen issues his apology letter saying there was a relationship.That’s not great for John Rizzo, Nvidia’s comms person. Tim Teter, Nvidia’s general counsel, is out there saying everything is above board. Now we know not everything is above board. What do you make of Nvidia’s corporate governance here? Because there’s a whole bunch of shareholder lawsuits to come. There’s one filed as of today. I can only imagine there are more to come.Nvidia has to tread very carefully here because what you don’t want is exactly what’s already happening, which is to start to deny or dismiss some of these issues and then turn around and have to say, “Actually, there might be something there.”This is especially important now as there are growing calls for a congressional investigation. So this is going to be separate, perhaps, from within the executive branch where, again, I think we have reasons to worry about conflicts of interest and people not wanting to do this all the way. But if there’s a full-blown congressional investigation, that might reveal some things that, if you are Nvidia, you want to get out in front of rather than have to backpedal later on and explain yourself.Part of the back and forth here with the government’s concern about Alice Huang and Megaspeed is that the Commerce Department spent months looking at the company and then Teter, the general counsel of Nvidia, emailed them and invoked a direct relationship with the Commerce undersecretary, Jeff Kessler. That got the case kicked to the DOJ where everything stopped.Trump yesterday said the FBI is investigating — that’s obviously connected to the DOJ. There’s a universe where the Trump administration is trying to make this go away. Nvidia can pressure the Trump administration to make this go away. That reeks of corruption, obviously.And then you have a very empowered class of Democrats coming into Congress with polling that suggested corruption was one of the top issues in this last election. I don’t see any outcome except those Democrats and an empowered bunch of investigators and an empowered bunch of committee chairs coming after Nvidia as hard as they can.How should the company think about that? Should they just fire Jensen now to get away from it? Should they put them in front of Congress every day for the next year? How do you think that’s going to play out?I think, at the most fundamental level, they need to cooperate and comply with calls from Congress to carry out this full investigation. Because up until now, this has all been so murky, and part of the reason why this has been a stop-and-go, even though those of us in the China AI space have been hearing about this for a while.Companies like Megaspeed, their role in all this, even people like Alice Huang, have been flagged much earlier than this. The fact that this is coming out now, but also that the investigation was stopped and started within the Trump administration, is a big red flag. Ultimately, from Nvidia’s standpoint, they’re going to have to come clean with whatever Congress now requests. There are going to be a lot of hard questions from Congress, as there should be, that have been building up for some time now.If you ever looked at Jensen’s approach to chip export controls, he’s been very fiery that chip export controls are stupid. You mentioned earlier that’s in his business interest. It is better for the Chinese AI industry to be dependent on CUDA and dependent on Nvidia chips, because then if we do get into some conflict, maybe you can restrict that access and you’ll set them back. There’s some swirl of argument that he makes that says it’s in the United States’ national security interest to ship as many Nvidia GPUs to China as you can.Then there are a lot of China hawks who are saying, “Actually, you need to restrain them and keep them years behind. They will not catch up to our bleeding-edge technology. Jensen, you just keep us ahead.” It feels like, out of all of this, the China hawks are going to start winning more fights than they’re losing — arguing that the Chinese government is actively trying to impede our efforts or actively trying to influence our government.How should people think about that? What framework should we use to evaluate that mass of differing opinions, especially now that there’s a catalyst for some kind of change?I think that’s the right way to frame up this whole debate. You have, on the one hand, folks who see the US-China AI competition as a critical strategic competition and access to compute is one of the key levers there, and thus US export controls, not only as they stand now, but tightening them further will be critical to maintaining US edge in the most powerful technology of our lives.Then there are other people who are in the opposite camp who advocate for greater exports of the US AI tech stack writ large, including Nvidia chips and including to China. Up until now, that camp has been led by people like [Commerce Secretary] Howard Lutnick, Jensen Huang, and Trump himself. What’s interesting is the balance of power, in terms of whose arguing gets more weight, has been shifting and will shift in light of this recent controversy.So here now those who have been advocating for more exports and fewer export controls, some of their arguments have been tainted by this process potentially, regardless of where the investigation goes.Then there’s a final variable in all this, which is China itself. That’s something that matters a lot in this discussion because in the background, China is doing two things. One, they’re trying to build their own chips and they’re sort of all-in on building a resilient semiconductor supply chain with their own, say, Huawei AI chips that their own AI companies can use. They will never really catch up. It looks highly unlikely, but they could develop good enough chips to replace the Nvidia ones that they have been dependent on for so long.The second big factor from China is retaliation. And this is one thing that I’m watching very closely. If these greater export controls are placed by the US on not just chips to China, but also on chip-making equipment — the tools required to make the semiconductors themselves — will China use its own export controls, such as restricting rare earth metals, to hit back?Right. This is in the context of an ongoing trade and tariff war that has rocked the United States’ economy. In many ways, the first thing that Democrats should do when they enter the next Congress is pass a law getting rid of all the Trump tariffs, right? They’re brought into Congress to fix affordability and the tariffs are an affordability problem, and now we’re going to rush into a trade war with China because we might ask the Dutch government to restrict ASML chip making machines.That seems very fraught to say, “We need to enter into an even more heated AI war with China that might result in the Chinese government placing export controls on the goods that you already find unaffordable.” Do you think that there’s the political will to go through this whole exercise, or is it just to punish Nvidia and Jensen Huang?In some ways, this is happening against the backdrop of other issues that are probably more top of mind for both voters and for incoming legislators in the Capitol. Things like cost of living, as you point out, tariffs, and trying to investigate the Trump administration more broadly for corruption and other issues. Somewhere in there is also the debate around data centers and AI itself.So in some ways, I’ll be curious to see how far this goes, the particular Nvidia issue. There is a scenario where a congressional investigation comes and goes, potentially finds no wrongdoing on Jensen Huang’s part, and then this is just folded into the longer debate around export controls. But there’s another world where if there are issues that come up, that could be potentially disruptive, not just for Nvidia and not just for the US-China relationship, but also for the AI boom in the US overall.Tell me more about China itself. You mentioned that their chips will maybe get good enough. There’s an argument that the models right now, the frontier models we have today, are actually good enough to disrupt the economy. They’re certainly good enough to disrupt the field of mathematics.You could stop training new models and just let the technology diffuse and you would still disrupt huge swaths of the economy today. We’re nowhere close to that actually happening. I think the AI labs should prove that they can do it with the technology they have today. That’s for another time.But China doesn’t need to compete at the frontier to gain the productivity advantages and to gain the industrial advantages. The example I keep using is 5G. I was told for a decade that we had to win the race to 5G, otherwise China would do something and no one would ever tell me what the “something” was.What is the “something” with AI that China will defeat us at that has made this such a critical geopolitical chess match? And is there a point where it will just be good enough for them to achieve that “something”?The funny thing is that China doesn’t see this AI race as being so much about the frontier per se. They’re really much more focused on diffusing the technology. And they think they can “win” the AI race by just having AI used much more broadly and integrated throughout the economy, especially in areas like manufacturing where they are already the behemoth.I think when they see the discussion around getting to AGI, certainly from the government standpoint in Beijing, that to them looks like a bubble and a waste of money. Why are you building all that compute for that? What’s interesting to see is the strategy as they’ve been playing it out is one where they’re trying to not fall too far behind the US, but really focus a lot more on trying to get — especially these open source models — out there across the Chinese economy and globally as well. To that extent, on that metric, they seem to be doing well.That, to me, always has seemed like the real fight. Anthropic and OpenAI are furious that the Chinese companies are constantly distilling their models. They’re trying to build some technology to keep them from distilling their models.But if you believe in the promise of AI and what it can do to the economy, your emphasis should be on diffusing good enough models, not AGI. Whereas our emphasis due to the way our market works is a bunch of guys who think they’re going to build digital Jesus. Whatever is going to happen, that’s the thing they want. [Anthropic CEO] Dario Amodei has to pretend that he cares about Salesforce, but we know what his real priority is.How do the United States and China compete in that dynamic, where you have one very managed economy that has set a much more near-term and potentially achievable goal, and then our market system where the incentives of the leading market players have nothing to do with the economic incentives of the rest of us?There’s even an ideological foundation to all of this because the vision of AGI is one that is so deeply embedded right now in the American AI community and Silicon Valley culture that I think there’s a risk of potential disconnect, not just between the US and China on this issue, but also within the US, between those who are in the labs like Anthropic and those who are outside who are saying, “Why are we building these giant metal boxes in our backyards? We don’t really see the point of this.”So there’s already that divergence there. Part of it is this longstanding obsession in the American AI imagination with getting to the machine god essentially.Bringing that all back to the context of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, Alice Huang, and Megaspeed. Megaspeed is a data center provider in Southeast Asia. It’s theoretically their business. They’re building data centers, they’re buying these chips. Shouldn’t market forces just end this?The United States AI companies want to build data centers. They will pay whatever rates because they have an ideological purpose that is disconnected from capitalism potentially. The Chinese government is just trying to diffuse AI into manufacturing and the United States government would like to hold them back.Shouldn’t market forces just mean that you sell the chips to the highest bidder and the highest bidder will almost always be an American AI company?That’s an interesting question, because there is ultimately market demand in China still for these Nvidia chips. And there’s a divergence here between the companies in China who still want access to Nvidia chips and the government who is saying, “No, no, no. Why don’t you try Chinese chips? Why don’t you help us with our Chinese domestic chip development?”There’s that divergence there. What’s interesting is players like Megaspeed in between could potentially do things like not just allow Chinese AI companies, again, to potentially get access to Nvidia chips, but then the argument some people are making is that those are chips that could have gone to the US AI companies and hyperscalers who are desperate.That is an argument that’s out there, but fundamentally, I don’t know how much of this is driven by those sheer commercial interests alone or, again, by some of these policy or ideological divides.Or by the influence of an alleged spy.Right, exactly.Because in a pure market environment, I think I know how this goes, but then you obviously have the complicated geopolitical dynamics and then you have this corruption element where both governments are attempting to influence one company at the center of the storm.What do you think happens if the Nvidia board investigation determines that Jensen acted inappropriately or a shareholder lawsuit imposes massive liability on Nvidia or a congressional investigation?There’s no way this company comes out of this unscathed, and the options are Jensen steps down or Nvidia’s restrained in some way or export controls go up even higher. Walk us through the probabilities and what you think happens next.There is a scenario actually where this ends up with not that much happening.Interesting.There is a pathway where there is a congressional investigation and they possibly find no wrongdoing or maybe Jensen really didn’t know, as he claims, that this Alice Huang person was a Chinese spy, and that this ends up feeding into the longer standing trajectory of all the export control debates and everything like that. That’s one possibility.Another possibility, though, is if there is some kind of wrongdoing that’s found, Jensen Huang might have to step down as CEO. He’s not just like a central node, he is like American AI, like the pillar that is holy.He’s the only one making the dollar. I mean, this is very important.Yeah, it’s like if you could draw the network diagram of the entire US AI ecosystem, Nvidia would be at the center of that. If you could draw the diagram of the entire Nvidia ecosystem, a single man is standing at the heart of all of that.The question becomes, if he were no longer the CEO of Nvidia, how much impact would that have on Nvidia’s ability to make progress on its own AI chips and what impact would that have on the rest of the US AI industry? One possibility, for example, is that there is a slowdown in Nvidia’s ability to crank out next generation after next generation of better and better chips. And that could impact US overall compute build out. That is one possibility.Another possibility is that there’s just so much demand and that the knowledge is diffused enough throughout Nvidia that the company can still continue to make progress at a breakneck pace even without their fearless leader at the top. A lot is unknown.“Fearless” is the right word, because when I look at Nvidia, again, I don’t think Jensen is designing the chips. I know that there’s a character he wants to play, where he’s in all the meetings and he’s probably taking some risk in chip design that is hard for us to see from the outside.But what we can see is Jensen’s enormous appetite for risk when it comes to financing neoclouds and investing in frontier AI companies. All of the dollars Nvidia is making flow back out in a circle to the AI ecosystem. It’s unclear to me whether that continues to happen without Jensen specifically being willing to front the risk and show up on CNBC as the face of the risk and say, “Everything’s okay.” What do you think happens then?His role as not just a technology leader, but as a market maker is really crucial. When he calls out certain companies like certain startups or neoclouds, you can see their stock prices go up. When he says something like, “I don’t know if this quantum thing is going to work out,” you saw the entire industry takes a hit. So that is the weight of his role in the broader ecosystem.Going forward, without that kind of advocate and this market maker playing this active role, that’s another factor. Beyond the Nvidia chips themselves and the technological role of the company, there is this deeper industry or even sociological function that Jensen plays and that Nvidia plays in this broader AI buildout.One of the interesting dynamics in all of that is Jensen also doesn’t seem to care very much about AGI. He thinks it’s just software. I’ve heard him say, “This is just software. Everybody calm down. These risks are fake. We don’t need a safety regime, all this stuff.” He’s more aligned with what you’re describing as the Chinese viewpoint, where this is just a tool to accelerate our economy. If he goes, maybe that changes too.It’s possible. He has been one of the most powerful counterweights to the “let’s go all in on AGI” perspective that you hear from Dario Amodei and Sam Altman, for example. Without his voice in that process, he’s also been a very strong advocate for open source. Again, emphasizing the diffusion rather than the, say, control and restrictions on cutting-edge AI.I do think if his voice is not there, there would be a pretty big vacuum for folks who would advocate that position or that view. At the same time though, again, beyond the immediate AI industry in the US, I don’t know how much that “race to AGI” argument resonates with the broader US public.Right now a lot of people are just more wondering about the nuts and bolts of it. Is this technology going to cost me my job tomorrow? Is it actually useful? Is it impacting my university studies? Those are things that maybe are more impactful day-to-day for most ordinary Americans.It is abundantly clear that Jensen is not a great spokesperson to the average consumer in the United States. He has not made the sale to them. He’s made the sale to a bunch of financiers. He’s made the sale to Wall Street. He’s made the sale to the tech industry.But the average American, as we can just see from the polling in the election, is very, very skeptical of all of this and very, very skeptical of the costs versus the benefits. Again, I’m just putting that in the context of there’s an alleged Chinese spy whispering in the ear of this man.What truly would the Chinese government hope to gain from that? Because in one way, they’ve actually achieved a victory here. They’ve destabilized the American AI economy. But it doesn’t seem like that was the goal. They’re furiously denying that any of this even happened.There is another very counterintuitive take, which is they kind of shot themselves in the foot on this one. From Beijing’s perspective, they don’t want to see more export controls, they might want to see a loosening. But now because of this potential Chinese spy, they’ve tainted the one man who has been advocating the most for loosening export controls. In some ways now, they’ve taken out someone who had otherwise for sheer commercial reasons been more aligned, and who’s going to take that place?If anything now, it has really charged the Democrats especially, who have been criticizing the Trump administration about not being tougher on these export controls. It has really galvanized the Democrats on this front and made it more of an issue perhaps than it was before.Yeah, especially when you connect it to corruption and the AI industry wasting money, all this stuff, it’s all there for them. Tell me more broadly about Chinese spying in the AI industry.There was a report, I don’t know, a few months ago that OpenAI was warning its employees that spies abound, that if suddenly attractive people appeared, be wary because they were probably spies. I love that. There’s just something about that that’s great.Obviously when it hits Jensen, it’s a different kind of story, especially with the national security implications and corruption implications. Give us a sense of what the spy trade is like on the ground for the average AI researcher.All I can say here is that they are juicy targets. For the US AI labs, anyone who’s involved with cutting-edge frontier AI, chip production, and chip design would be juicy targets for Chinese intelligence gathering because this is something where China’s trying to catch up. They’re trying to figure out how to keep pace with the US on AI and try to build their own alternatives to Nvidia GPUs.You can see there have been other examples of cases where they’ve been poaching engineers from TSMC in Taiwan or from South Korea, and have struggled to deal with efforts to hold back this strategic IP basically. There’s probably a lot more happening under the surface in terms of this cat-and-mouse game, but I do think that they are prime targets.Correct me if I’m wrong, but I think that there have been warnings from the US government to be careful and to step up your game on the cybersecurity front and the intelligence front to protect against these threats.Meanwhile, they’re putting all their information into Slack and getting breached on the daily. Who knows if these warnings are taking off.Onto the last set of questions here — I’m thinking about Apple and Tesla, where we moved our manufacturing to China and we moved our supply chains to China, the Chinese industries.Whether it was above board or not — and there’s a rich debate you could have on that, we’ve had it on the show — they learned a lot from our companies. There was technology transfer. That’s happening in AI too.There are a lot of Chinese AI researchers working in and around these labs. There is technology transfer happening, again, above board or not. Isn’t that just the normal course of business or is there something more nefarious happening here?To some extent there are people flows and knowledge flows. You might not even think of it in terms of national-level AI communities. You might think about this global diffusion of know-how tips and tricks for squeezing a bit more performance out of the same amount of compute. Especially up until recently, you saw a lot of sharing of, say, papers like the transformer paper, that disseminated new architectural breakthroughs throughout the global AI community. And now that’s changing, obviously, as a lot of companies, especially the US companies, are holding this much closer to their chest.But there is this broader question about who gets access to this. Who gains and loses? I guess it’s also not just a one-way flow. Some of these American AI companies benefit a lot from having some of these Chinese developers work with them. In the same way Apple and Tesla, it wasn’t just like they gave away the crown jewels to China, but that China in turn saved these companies, especially at times when they were facing a perilous moment in their histories.There’s this bigger question about what the line is between normal commercial and technology flows versus a concerted state-backed effort to obtain sensitive strategic secrets and IP technology that would have broader geopolitical implications.Does that strategy for China look like a bunch of companies like Megaspeed with allegedly compromised executives, or does it play out more directly?Actually if anything, it would be less about the companies like Megaspeed, who seem to be middlemen for dealing with compute, and perhaps different companies, different agencies perhaps in the Chinese system, that might be more active.At one extreme you have the outright concerted efforts at industrial espionage. They’re state-backed actors who are very systematic at trying to obtain some of the best commercial secrets from around the world, including from American companies.But on the other hand, you do also have this gray zone of, “If a Chinese company acquires a stake in a US or European company, what does that mean? Does that mean they’re trying to obtain the technology or is that a regular commercial deal?” That’s where it starts to get more difficult to parse and you’d have to look at it on a case-by-case basis.One of the dynamics in talking about the Chinese government and the United States, especially when you talk to American industrialists, is that the American government is chaos and democracy is messy and everyone’s running in 50 different directions, and the Chinese system is directed. They make 100-year plans, not one-quarter plans. We’ve heard it. Everyone knows these cliches.How true is that? In this case alone, it doesn’t seem like they achieved the goal of their plan. In many cases, they might have actually set themselves back.Oh, yeah. For those who actually study China, who have done long-term research on this country and who understand it more closely, it looks like a much messier picture than any of these portrayals, especially from those in Silicon Valley who try to juxtapose China against what they find to be this annoyingly messy and unruly democracy.The Chinese system, both within the government and then across industries and government, is full of conflicting interests, rife with corruption. You see the local governments not following what Beijing wants, or following what Beijing wants but in the wrong direction. history.titleZh: 黄仁勋出局了。中国想从他那里得到什么？
history.descriptionZh:
这期 The Verge《Decoder》播客以“紧急更新”开场，称 Nvidia CEO 黄仁勋在节目发布前数分钟被报道已辞去 CEO，原因与其绯闻及一名疑似中国间谍 Alice Huang 有关，事件可能进一步吞噬公司；但节目同时说明，对 Kyle Chan 的访谈是两天前录制的，当时黄仁勋的去留仍未知。播客随后与布鲁金斯学会约翰·桑顿中国中心研究员 Kyle Chan 讨论事件核心：中国若在黄仁勋身边安插间谍究竟想得到什么，以及美中 AI 竞争的真实状态。需要强调，文中对 Alice Huang 和 Megaspeed 的指控均为“疑似/报道”，尚无司法结论。

事件背景方面，Alice Huang 被指可能是中国情报资产，同时是 Nvidia 客户 Megaspeed 的高管。Megaspeed 在马来西亚建设数据中心，可能与中企有联系，并可能成为中企间接获取 Blackwell 等先进 Nvidia 芯片的通道。报道还称，美国情报机构一年前已向特朗普政府标记相关风险，卢比奥看过备忘录；商务部调查 Megaspeed 数月后，Nvidia 总法律顾问 Tim Teter 邮件联系商务部副部长 Jeff Kessler，案件被转至司法部后停滞，特朗普称 FBI 正在调查。与此同时，Nvidia 对外先称关系正常，黄仁勋后又发道歉信承认存在关系，公司治理和股东诉讼风险上升，国会调查呼声增强。播客认为，无论最终是否发现不当行为，Nvidia 都很难毫发无伤。

技术与产业逻辑上，中国 AI 公司长期依赖 Nvidia GPU 和 CUDA 生态，甚至成为 CUDA 生态的重要贡献者；美国出口管制推动其转向华为等国产 AI 芯片，目标是建立“够用”、不一定立刻比肩 Nvidia 最先进产品、但对华盛顿政策更具韧性的平行供应链。节目以 DeepSeek R1 为例：其某些方面表现优于美国模型，但并非完全没有芯片，而是在已有芯片上做了大量微调，说明中国未必要最高端芯片也能取得进展。Megaspeed 这类中间商则可能让中国 AI 公司间接获得 Blackwell，并挤占美国超大规模客户急需的芯片供应。原文没有给出算力、带宽、能效、成本等具体性能参数，也没有量化对比数据；相关比较均为定性描述，如 Blackwell 是前沿芯片、华为等国产芯片“够用但未必比肩”、CUDA 形成生态锁定等。

关于中国动机，Kyle Chan 认为可能有两层：一是获取美国政策过程信息，二是通过黄仁勋影响美国出口管制。黄仁勋与特朗普关系密切，特朗普可随时打其手机，因此北京可能最看重“能在正确耳边低语的人”。但矛盾在于，Nvidia 已与 Megaspeed 有业务关系，黄仁勋本人也一直为商业利益游说放宽对华芯片出口，北京未必需要再推；另一种可能是北京只想要“可见性”和情报。事件还可能反噬中国：它污染了最主张放宽出口管制的人，强化民主党在国安、腐败和 AI 浪费问题上的攻势。美国内部两派——视算力为战略竞争关键、主张收紧管制的鹰派，与包括 Lutnick、黄仁勋和特朗普在内、主张扩大美国 AI 技术栈出口的阵营——力量平衡可能因此向鹰派倾斜。中国则在双轨应对：一边建国产芯片供应链，一边可能以稀土等出口管制反制美国收紧芯片及设备限制。

技术影响和应用场景上，Nvidia 位于整个美国 AI 金融生态中心，黄仁勋有约 60 名直接下属，既是技术领导者也是“市场做市者”，其言论能影响初创公司、neocloud 和行业股价；若他下台，可能影响 Nvidia 下一代芯片迭代节奏和美国算力建设，也可能因知识扩散而继续推进。黄仁勋还是 AGI 怀疑者和开源扩散派，认为 AI 只是软件，与 Dario Amodei、Sam Altman 等“全押 AGI”路线形成制衡；若他离开，这一立场可能出现真空。中国则更重视把“够用”的 AI 扩散到制造业和全球经济，视 AGI 竞赛为泡沫和浪费，类似 5G 竞争，真正胜负可能在开源模型和广泛部署，而非前沿 AGI。播客最后判断，后续可能路径包括国会调查未发现重大不当、事件并入出口管制辩论；或发现不当导致黄仁勋下台、Nvidia 受限、出口管制进一步收紧。值得关注国会调查、出口管制法案、白宫态度以及中国反制。

history.title: Google reworks TPU silicon into specialized systems for agents and security
history.description: Google’s TPU 8i Max and TPU 8tx reuse TPU 8i and TPU 8t silicon to target long-context agents and confidential inference.
history.content: Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Google's eighth-generation TPU family has now expanded further. Back in April, the company announced TPU 8t for training AI models and TPU 8i for general-purpose inference workloads. Google has now introduced TPU 8tx, built on the same silicon as the previously announced 8t, for confidential, hardware-isolated inference aimed at regulated enterprises and governments, and TPU 8i Max, which combines two 8i chips on one package for long-context agentic work.TPU 8tx swaps the Arm-based Axion hosts of the 8t and 8i for a 5th Gen AMD EPYC CPU, adopting a Boardfly network, and the 8i Max doubles the compute, SRAM, and HBM bandwidth of the original 8i. The original split, the TPU 8t and 8i, made natural sense. The 8t targets large-scale training, while the 8i leans toward low-latency inference and reasoning. TPUs have become a fast-growing business, with the company claiming nearly 100 customers, including Meta’s recent move to TPUs. The more modular approach is flexible and can deliver specialized systems “in a matter of months rather than years,” helping that popularity along. (Image credit: Google) Swipe to scroll horizontally Google’s eighth-generation TPU systems Header Cell - Column 0 TPU 8t TPU 8i TPU 8tx TPU 8i Max Built for Large-scale pre-training Sampling, serving and reasoning Secure, confidential inference; small-scale training Long-context agent work Silicon TPU 8t TPU 8i Same silicon as TPU 8t Two TPU 8i chips on one package Host CPU Arm Axion Arm Axion 5th Gen AMD EPYC Not stated Network 3D torus Boardfly Boardfly Not stated Peak FP4 PFLOPS 12.6 10.1 Not stated About 20.2 (derived) HBM bandwidth (GB/s) 6,528 8,601 Not stated About 17,202 (derived) HBM capacity (GB) 216 288 Not stated Not stated On-chip SRAM (MB) 128 384 Not stated 768 (derived) Availability Coming soon Coming soon Coming soon Coming soon For the new parts, the TPU 8i Max isn't innovative on the surface, as it’s just two TPU 8i chips combined into a single package. The result is twice the theoretical compute, but more importantly, it fits twice the silicon within the “existing rack footprint,” and Google claims more compute per square foot and per watt.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: Doubling both SRAM and HBM bandwidth helps keep things scaling, which would put the 8i Max at about 20.2 FP4 PFLOPS, 768 MB SRAM, and about 17.2 TB/s HBM bandwidth. This compares to Nvidia’s Rubin R200 GPU at a rated 50 FP4 PFLOPS for inference and 22 TB/s of HBM4 per socket, or AMD’s MI455X with 40 FP4 PFLOPS. The compute gap is closing.The memory bandwidth doubling is also potentially one way around moving to HBM4. The memory wall, as Google calls it, or the bandwidth bottleneck, is a real concern “when dozens of AI agents work together across an entire software codebase.” Larger context windows — with larger models targeting 1 million tokens — mean larger KV caches, partly held in SRAM, and each new token has to read that cache back from memory, which is where the extra HBM bandwidth helps. It’s a different route from Nvidia’s LPX: more bandwidth in one package, rather than a second chip type for decoding and a storage tier for context. You may like Google reportedly taps AMD to design next-generation TPU Google’s TPUs for AI workloads now run in Meta's data centers Hot Chips 2026: Nvidia presents Groq 3 LPX architecture and unveils its first third-party inference benchmark Google also provides useful software for agents to get the most out of its hardware. TPU Sync is an open-source “model-state layer for TPU clusters” that moves KV caches off the chip’s HBM, “automatically tiering massive KV caches off the chip in milliseconds” down to host DRAM and, experimentally, shared storage. Google says this can cut KV transfer latency by “more than 90%,” with time-to-first-token gains that vary by workload. The company has also announced the Agent Compute Engine, a Google Cloud service that pauses idle agent sessions and moves their working memory aside until they’re needed again, another memory-saving effort.Google credits its vLLM-TorchTPU stack with “state-of-the-art price-performance marks” on InferenceX and AgentX, which test realistic agentic coding and long-context work. However, the only published third-party numbers so far are for the last-generation Ironwood TPU. In SemiAnalysis’s InferenceX tests in September, running Qwen3.5 397B in FP8, Ironwood delivered 50.4% more tokens per dollar than Nvidia’s B200 and 96.0% more than the B300 at 20 tokens per second per user. One issue with that, however, is that Ironwood lacks native FP4, although newer November results show its FP8 beating Nvidia’s FP4 GB300 NVL72 on the same model, at 1.67 times the performance per dollar. There is also no eighth-gen result yet to compare how the new generation differs.In contrast to the 8i Max, which is designed for long-context work, the new TPU 8tx, “built on the same silicon as TPU 8t,” is “optimized for secure and confidential inference” as well as small-scale training. The security is built into the hardware with isolation to prevent snooping on sensitive data, including model weights. Normally, data has to be unlocked in memory during processing, which is the step this isolation is meant to cover.This chip is intended for areas where security and confidentiality are high priorities, which means regulated enterprises and governments, particularly those who are using frontier or proprietary models. In that case, the operators may want to “fine-tune models using their private data, distill large models into smaller ones, and train their agents,” without having to move sensitive data between clusters. Agents and security meet here for “secure agent execution.” Back in April, the Pentagon and Google reportedly held discussions for TPU usage in classified settings, although the 8tx chip is not specifically named.Google’s Private AI Compute, its “hardened TPU platform” with protections “comparable to a typical TEE,” per its September technical brief, already runs confidential serving on TPUs. The 8tx appears to be that capability turned into a product for customers. Alternatives include Nvidia’s NVL72, with one security domain across 72 Rubin GPUs, 36 Vera CPUs, and the interconnects, and Intel’s TDX, which is adding trusted I/O to cover data moving to accelerators. What to read next OpenAI’s Jalapeño ASICs are deployed alongside AMD EPYC ‘Turin’ CPUs as hosts, not Nvidia's Vera Tesla unveils AI accelerator roadmap, adopts new 'SI' branding in 'Super Intelligence' push Hot Chips 2026: OpenAI's Jalapeño AI ASIC unpacked The TPU 8tx hosts are based on 5th Gen AMD EPYC boards, instead of the Axion hosts on the 8t, which replaced x86 in April. There's one Axion for every two TPUs on the 8i, compared with one Xeon per four on Ironwood. Google gives no reason for the change, but its Confidential VM configuration list has both AMD and Intel series chips, with no Arm-based ones listed. Private AI Compute uses “an AMD-based hardware Trusted Execution Environment” for its CPU workloads, suggesting Google swapped something it already runs on its confidential stack.The 8tx also adopts the 8i’s Boardfly network over the 8t’s torus, which Google claims can deliver “up to 2x lower latency compared to TPU 8t” with almost no performance penalty, although it’s not clear what measure Google is using. The alternative torus network suits training, since chips mostly swap data with neighbors in a predictable manner, but inference on large mixture-of-experts and reasoning models can send smaller messages between distant chips, with every hop adding delay. With Boardfly, it’s at most seven hops against 16 at 1,024 chips.What is lacking is a full specifications table, the amount of HBM capacity, pod sizes, an availability date, pricing, and customers for either system. Details on attestation, that is, the ability for the customer to verify confidentiality, are also missing for 8tx. The 8tx and 8i Max are currently listed, along with the 8i and 8t, as “coming soon” on Google’s Cloud TPU page.Delivering two new TPU systems nearly seven months after April’s pair shows Google wants to turn out specialized systems much more quickly than has been the case in the past. Now, it just needs to prove them, through benchmarks and an availability date when the hardware is actually in customers’ hands.

history.titleZh: 谷歌将TPU芯片改造为面向智能体与安全的专用系统
history.descriptionZh:
Google 第八代 TPU 家族在原有 TPU 8t 和 TPU 8i 基础上进一步扩展，新增 TPU 8tx 和 TPU 8i Max，分别面向高安全隔离推理与长上下文智能体工作负载。今年 4 月，Google 发布第八代 TPU 时，将产品线按用途拆分为面向大规模预训练的 TPU 8t 和面向通用推理、采样与服务的 TPU 8i。此次新增的两款产品延续了这种模块化思路：用相对较少的硅片和系统改动，在数月而非数年内推出针对特定场景的专用系统。Google 称 TPU 业务增长迅速，已有近 100 家客户，Meta 近期也开始采用 TPU。

TPU 8i Max 的核心思路是把两颗 TPU 8i 芯片封装在同一个 package 中，从表面看只是“双芯封装”，但实际意义在于在不增加现有机架占地的情况下放入两倍硅片，并提升每平方英尺和每瓦算力。根据翻倍关系推算，TPU 8i Max 约达到 20.2 FP4 PFLOPS、768MB 片上 SRAM 和约 17.2TB/s HBM 带宽；相比之下，单颗 TPU 8i 为 10.1 FP4 PFLOPS、384MB SRAM、8,601GB/s HBM 带宽和 288GB HBM 容量。Google 没有公布 8i Max 的完整规格和 HBM 容量，但强调其面向长上下文智能体任务，双倍 SRAM 和 HBM 带宽有助于维持扩展性。与 Nvidia Rubin R200 的 50 FP4 PFLOPS 推理算力和每 socket 22TB/s HBM4 带宽，以及 AMD MI455X 的 40 FP4 PFLOPS 相比，Google 的算力差距正在缩小。

长上下文和智能体负载的关键瓶颈之一是“内存墙”，也就是带宽瓶颈。当数十个 AI 智能体在整个软件代码库上协同工作时，模型需要更大的上下文窗口，目标可达 100 万 token，这会带来更大的 KV cache；其中一部分放在 SRAM，但每生成一个新 token 都要从内存读回缓存，因此额外 HBM 带宽十分重要。Google 的路线与 Nvidia 的 LPX 不同：它不是增加第二种用于解码的芯片和面向上下文的存储层级，而是在单个 package 内提供更高带宽。软件层面，Google 推出开源 TPU Sync，作为 TPU 集群的“模型状态层”，可把海量 KV cache 自动分层迁移到主机 DRAM，并实验性扩展到共享存储，迁移可在毫秒级完成，Google 称可将 KV 传输延迟降低 90% 以上，首 token 时延收益因负载而异。此外，Agent Compute Engine 可暂停空闲智能体会话并移出其工作内存，进一步节省内存。Google 还称其 vLLM-TorchTPU 软件栈在 InferenceX 和 AgentX 上取得领先的性价比，但目前公开的第三方数据仍来自上一代 Ironwood：SemiAnalysis 9 月测试中，Ironwood 运行 Qwen3.5 397B FP8、在每用户每秒 20 token 条件下，每美元 token 数比 Nvidia B200 高 50.4%，比 B300 高 96.0%；11 月结果还显示其 FP8 在相同模型上性价比达到 Nvidia FP4 GB300 NVL72 的 1.67 倍。不过，目前还没有第八代 TPU 的第三方对比结果。

TPU 8tx 则与 TPU 8t 基于同一硅片，重点针对安全、机密推理以及小规模训练。其安全能力构建在硬件隔离中，防止敏感数据和模型权重被窥探；通常数据在处理时需要在内存在解锁，而该隔离机制正是为了覆盖这一环节。该芯片面向对安全和保密要求高的受监管企业和政府机构，尤其是使用前沿或专有模型的客户。这类用户可能希望用私有数据微调模型、把大模型蒸馏为小模型、训练自己的智能体，同时不必在集群之间移动敏感数据，并可实现“安全的智能体执行”。今年 4 月曾有报道称美国国防部与 Google 讨论在机密环境中使用 TPU，但当时并未具体点名 8tx。Google 的 Private AI Compute 作为加固 TPU 平台，保护能力据称可与典型 TEE 相比，已在 TPU 上运行机密服务；8tx 可视为将这一能力产品化。竞争方案包括 Nvidia NVL72，其在 72 颗 Rubin GPU、36 颗 Vera CPU 及互连上形成一个安全域，以及 Intel TDX 通过可信 I/O 覆盖向加速器移动的数据。

系统设计上，TPU 8tx 没有沿用 8t 和 8i 的 Arm Axion 主机 CPU，而改用第五代 AMD EPYC，并采用 Boardfly 网络。Google 未解释更换原因，但其 Confidential VM 配置列表包含 AMD 和 Intel 系列芯片，没有 Arm 产品；Private AI Compute 的 CPU 工作负载也使用基于 AMD 的硬件 TEE，说明 Google 可能复用了既有 confidential 栈。网络方面，8tx 采用 8i 的 Boardfly，而非 8t 的 3D torus。Google 称 Boardfly 相比 TPU 8t 可带来最高 2 倍更低延迟，且几乎没有性能损失，但未说明具体衡量指标。Torus 更适合训练，因为芯片主要以可预测方式与邻居交换数据；而大型 MoE 和推理模型在推理时会向远距离芯片发送较小消息，每一跳都会增加延迟。在 1,024 颗芯片规模下，Boardfly 最多 7 跳，而 torus 为 16 跳。

总体来看，Google 在 4 月发布 8t 和 8i 后不到七个月又推出 8tx 和 8i Max，表明其希望比过去更快地交付专用 TPU 系统。TPU 8i Max 通过双芯封装和双倍内存带宽强化长上下文智能体场景，TPU 8tx 则把机密计算硬件隔离、AMD EPYC 主机和 Boardfly 网络结合，瞄准受监管行业与政府市场。不过，两款产品目前均标注为“即将推出”，Google 尚未公布完整规格、HBM 容量、pod 规模、上市日期、价格和客户，8tx 的远程证明等机密性验证细节也缺失。接下来，Google 需要通过第三方基准测试和实际交付时间来证明这些新系统的价值。

history.title: Struggling marijuana farms pivot to becoming AI data center sites to escape falling weed revenue
history.description: One expert says that it still depends on the perfect confluence of cheap power, favorable regulation, and reliable connectivity.
history.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 4 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter The AI data center boom is bringing hope to struggling cannabis farmers as they face increased competition, costs, and taxes amid reduced demand for marijuana. According to Arizona Public Media, the cannabis industry is in decline, with sales peaking in 2024 and oversupply driving prices down. And now, several growers are considering selling their cultivation facilities or converting them into “mini data center nodes.” These facilities already have many of the ingredients needed for AI data centers, such as the increasingly hard-to-get supply of electricity and water infrastructure."For some reason, there's a lot more cannabis grown in Arizona than Arizonans use. And so, a lot of folks are getting out of that business, like myself, at least on the cultivation side. But these facilities can potentially be repurposed to be mini data center nodes," Moe Asnani, the former owner of two Tucson D2 Dispensaries, told the public broadcaster. He also added, "The whole idea is if you create these smaller nodes where people control their own data, where they're not at the mercy of other people's updates and things like that — that's kind of where the idea came in, because I believe in decentralization."Cannabis farming is both power- and water-intensive. Forbes looked at a 32,850-square-foot cannabis facility in Kalamazoo, Michigan, which is currently wired for 1.5 megawatts, which can be expanded to 2.5 megawatts in under a year and 15 megawatts in the long term. It's also provisioned for fiber internet and equipped with a state-of-the-art HVAC system for climate control, which should make it a tempting property for anyone wanting to put up a small data center — something that even OpenAI and Anthropic are interested in as massive hyperscale sites face opposition from the community.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: This concept is dubbed "adaptive reuse," with Tucson City Council member Paul Cunningham saying that it’s a more palatable alternative to massive, purpose-built sites sitting on the outskirts of town. "Data centers are dirty words, and everybody knows that. And no one wants to build a brand-new data center anywhere," the politician said. "But if we have buildings that were using that amount of water and that amount of energy already in their previous function and [it] can be done without being invasive, I'm OK with exploring that option."There is massive demand for data centers, but it’s not a guaranteed payoff for struggling cash-strapped growers looking to unload their unprofitable properties. Niki Krear, vice president of acquisitions of real estate investment trust New Lake Capital Partners, said that there’s a sweet spot between connectivity, costs, and regulation that data center operators look for in a site. You may like China shifting massive AI data center complexes to rural provinces to tap surplus energy OpenAI and Anthropic scramble for smaller data centers as massive gigawatt projects lag Nvidia eyes converting old nuclear plants into massive AI data centers "It’s a combination of finding affordable power, dense fiber networks, and favorable tax policies," Krear told MJBizDaily. Even though many cultivation facilities already boast higher-than-average power capacity for lighting and climate control, data centers often demand twice to thrice more, with upgrades possibly taking up to five years.Data center operators looking for smaller sites may also have to contend with NIMBY — not in my backyard — fights from neighbors. Additionally, there may be zoning restrictions, moratoriums, and regulatory hurdles, and the lack of economies of scale could end up costing operators more.Stay On the Cutting Edge: Get the Tom's Hardware NewsletterGet Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.Contact me with news and offers from other Future brandsReceive email from us on behalf of our trusted partners or sponsorsThis is particularly important as AI chips are expected to increase in power and efficiency in the next five years. As these new AI GPUs become available, data centers will need to sell their existing equipment and buy new hardware to remain competitive. Because suppliers usually offer favorable pricing for larger orders, upgrading these smaller sites will likely end up being more expensive on a per-unit basis. That said, growing opposition toward large new projects could make these former cannabis farms suitable alternatives for operators desperate to get more compute online quickly, provided they check all (or most of) the boxes they need. history.titleZh: 挣扎中的大麻农场转型为AI数据中心场地，以摆脱大麻收入下滑
history.descriptionZh:
美国AI数据中心建设热潮正为处境艰难的大麻种植者带来新的出路。由于大麻销售在2024年见顶、供过于求导致价格下跌，加上竞争、成本和税负上升，亚利桑那等地出现种植设施过剩，一些种植者开始考虑出售种植场，或将其改造成“迷你数据中心节点”。这一思路被称为“适应性再利用”（adaptive reuse）：不再在城郊新建大型专用数据中心，而是利用现有大麻种植设施改建小型算力节点。支持者认为，这类建筑已经具备数据中心所需的不少条件，包括越来越难获得的电力接入、供水基础设施、光纤互联网以及用于控温的先进HVAC系统，因此改造可能比从零新建更容易被社区接受。

从设施条件看，大麻种植本身属于高耗电、高耗水行业，其电力容量通常高于普通建筑。报道以密歇根州卡拉马祖一处32,850平方英尺的大麻设施为例：该设施目前接入1.5兆瓦电力，可在不到一年内扩展到2.5兆瓦，长期可扩展至15兆瓦，并已具备光纤接入和先进气候控制系统。这些条件使其对希望部署小型数据中心的主体具有一定吸引力。图森市议员Paul Cunningham表示，大型数据中心常被视为“脏词”，社区对新建项目抵触明显；但如果既有建筑过去已经消耗同等规模的水和能源，且改造不具侵入性，他愿意探索这种方案。前大麻店主Moe Asnani则强调，小型节点可让人们控制自己的数据，不必受制于他人更新，体现去中心化理念。与此同时，OpenAI和Anthropic等AI公司也在寻找较小规模的数据中心，因为超大规模项目面临社区反对和落地延迟。

不过，这一转型并非稳赚。数据中心运营商选址通常看重廉价电力、密集光纤网络和有利税收政策的组合。大麻种植设施虽然电力容量高于平均水平，但数据中心往往需要其2至3倍的电力，电力升级可能耗时长达5年。小型站点还可能遭遇“邻避”反对、分区限制、暂停令和监管障碍；缺乏规模经济也会推高运营成本。尤其未来五年AI芯片功率和效率预计持续提升，数据中心需要出售旧设备、采购新硬件以保持竞争力，而供应商通常对大额订单给予优惠，小型站点的单位升级成本可能更高。

总体来看，将闲置大麻种植设施改造成小型AI数据中心节点，是一种基础设施再利用和分布式算力布局的探索。它的优势在于盘活现有高耗能、高耗水设施，缩短选址和建设周期，并可能缓解大型数据中心面临的社区阻力；应用场景包括边缘计算、小型AI算力节点和强调数据自主控制的分布式数据中心。但其成败取决于电力扩容、光纤连接、监管许可、税收条件和改造成本能否达到运营商要求。在大型新建项目受阻、算力需求又快速增长的背景下，前大麻农场可能成为急于快速上线算力的运营商的替代选项，但前提是这些设施能够满足数据中心选址所需的大部分关键条件。
